description: We are GeoHarmonics, a team of first-year B.Tech engineers who believe Earth’s story shouldn’t only be seen; it should be heard. We combine data science, audio engineering and cosmic curiosity to give planetary phenomena a voice: a warming ocean, a shrinking forest or a passing storm becomes rhythm, pitch and texture. We help Earth science become multi-sensory, inclusive and easier to remember.
summary:
Earth Jukebox turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualizations (ocean heat, lightning, aerosols, CO₂, night lights, forest height and currents) into live music generated from their pixels.

How it works:

Each frame is drawn to a canvas and analysed in real time.
Pixel colours are matched to the visualization's own colour bar with a nearest-neighbour search in a precomputed 32³ RGB lookup cube, recovering real values: °C, ppm, metres. Shaded imagery is compared by brightness-free colour (chroma) so shadows don't change the value.
Equirectangular projection maths converts each pixel to a latitude and longitude.
A 16-step scanner sweeps west to east, with stereo pan following longitude.
Values are snapped to musical scales, a voice limit, compressor and limiter keep busy data clean, and new lightning flashes are found by comparing successive frames.
Everything is synthesised with the Web Audio API.
Accessibility first:

Explore mode: blind and low-vision users move a sound probe by touch or keyboard and hear values and places spoken aloud.
Guidance: a guided story, an audio legend, screen-reader live descriptions and a mixer explain every sound.
details:
Project details: Earth Jukebox (GeoHarmonics)

What it does

Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live music generated from their pixels. You pick a "record" (one of seven NASA Scientific Visualization Studio visualizations) and the animation plays while a soundtrack is synthesised in real time from the frame on screen:

  • Ocean Heat & Currents (sea surface temperature)
  • Storm Drums (lightning seen from the ISS)
  • Air Quartet (GEOS aerosols)
  • Carbon Breath (DYAMOND CO₂)
  • City Lights (night lights 2012–2023)
  • Canopy (GEDI forest height)
  • Gulf Stream Tour (Perpetual Ocean 2)

There are five ways to use it:

  • Listen: the live sonification.
  • Guided story: a spoken introduction, then playback.
  • Hear the legend: what "low" and "high" sound like before you listen.
  • Explore by touch: pause and move a sound probe over the map with a finger, mouse or arrow keys; press Enter to hear something like "29.5 °C, near the Western Pacific Warm Pool".
  • Your image: upload any frame and sonify it.

How it works (pipeline, algorithms and math)

1. Media preparation. A Python pipeline streams the original SVS videos with ffmpeg, re-encodes them to 1024-pixel-wide H.264, and samples each visualization's own colour bar into a 96-step colour scale with the physical value at each end (0–32 °C, 380–460 ppm, 0–50 m, and so on).

2. Reading the frame. Several times per second, on every musical step, the current video frame is drawn to a canvas at a small analysis size (128×64, or 256×128 for lightning) and its pixels are read.

3. Turning colours back into data (colour-bar inversion). Each pixel is matched to the nearest colour on the visualization's legend, and its position t gives the value: value = v₀ + t·(v₁ − v₀). To run this on every frame, we precompute a 32×32×32 lookup cube (32,768 cells), so each pixel is a single table read. We use three distance measures:

  • RGB: plain Euclidean distance, for flat colour fields.
  • Chroma-normalised: each colour is divided by its brightest channel (c / max(R,G,B)) before comparing, so shadows and darker flow lines don't change the value. Used for shaded imagery such as ocean particles.
  • Hybrid: chroma plus a weighted lightness term, for GEDI's brown → green → cream scale, where height is mostly encoded in brightness.

Colours too far from every legend colour are rejected as "not data" (land, background, labels).

4. Location. Most records are equirectangular maps, so each pixel has a coordinate:
lat = 90 − (y+½)/H·180, lon = −180 + (x+½)/W·360.
Centres of activity (where the dust, smoke or plumes are) use a circular mean of longitude, atan2(Σ w·sin λ, Σ w·cos λ), so they stay correct across the date line. Coarse latitude/longitude boxes turn coordinates into place names.

5. Dataset-specific detection:

  • Lightning: a "yellowness" score, (R+G)/2 − B. A new flash is a cell lit now that was dark in the previous frame. The app also tracks the Northern-Hemisphere share and the busiest 30°×30° region.
  • Aerosols: a rule-based colour classifier (hue, saturation, brightness) sorts pixels into dust, smoke/black carbon, sea salt and sulfate.
  • Night lights: brightness is normalised per year. On the change map, gain versus loss gives a balance = (gain − loss)/(gain + loss).
  • CO₂: only the opaque 425–460 ppm part of the legend is inverted, because lower values are drawn transparent.
  • Motion: the mean absolute brightness difference between frames drives "flow" sounds.

6. The scanner (data to time and space). Every bar of music sweeps the map from west to east in 16 steps. Step k reads column k, so time in the bar and left–right stereo position both mean longitude, on every record. Each step summarises its column as a 16×12 grid of mean, maximum and coverage values.

7. Data to music.

  • Pitch: values are mapped onto a musical scale with a monotonic quantiser: k = round(t·N·octaves), MIDI note = root + 12⌊k/N⌋ + scale[k mod N], frequency = 440·2^((m−69)/12). A higher value never gives a lower note, and every note fits the harmony.
    • subtractive pads (detuned sawtooth waves through a low-pass filter with a slow wobble)
    • FM bells
    • drums (a sine wave with a falling pitch, plus band-passed noise)
    • noise grains for smoke and wind
  • Mixing: convolution reverb with a generated impulse response, a compressor and limiter, a 28-voice budget so dense data never turns into noise, and a look-ahead scheduler for tight timing.

8. Calibrating dates from the data. The lightning video's pace is uneven. We measured the Northern-Hemisphere lightning share every second of the video; it peaks once per boreal summer, so we pinned those peaks to mid-July and map video time to dates in straight-line segments between them.

9. Accessibility.

  • Sentences generated from the data go to a screen-reader live region and to optional browser text-to-speech.
  • Full keyboard control.
  • Vibration on supported phones for extremes and lightning.
  • High-contrast, larger-text and reduced-motion modes.
  • A layout that works from 320 px phones to 2560 px monitors.

Benefits

  • EIC visualizations are currently sight-only. Earth Jukebox lets blind and low-vision people explore Earth data independently, not just hear a summary.
  • Sound reveals patterns that are easy to miss by eye: storms following the sun, India brightening, plumes pulsing day and night.
  • It runs in any browser with no install and no account, and can be recorded as audio to make playlists.

Intended impact

  • An accessible, emotional way into climate and Earth science, usable on EIC displays, in classrooms and museums, and on phones.
  • It shows that NASA's existing visualization library can be made multi-sensory without new data products, and the method works on any colour-bar visualization (the "Your image" mode).

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, Python.
  • Browser APIs: Web Audio, Canvas 2D, Web Speech, Vibration, MediaRecorder.
  • Media pipeline: Python with ffmpeg (via imageio-ffmpeg), NumPy and Pillow.
  • Testing and serving: Node.js (a small static server with seeking support, and the built-in test runner, 23 tests on real NASA frames), plus headless Chrome for checking layouts across screen sizes.
  • Hosting: Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop and headphones. No special hardware.
  • AI: code written with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant, under our direction.
  • No third-party runtime libraries.

How it is creative

  • It plays the data, not the colours. Every note traces back to a real value through NASA's own legend.
  • The scanner gives one consistent sense of space across all records, and each dataset has its own instrumentation: a quartet of particle types, storm drums, a carbon "breath" that grows tense, cities as arpeggios.
  • Data shapes musical mood as well as pitch: the seasons through major/minor changes, and climate tension through detuning and darker scales.
  • Explore mode turns a picture into a playable instrument you can feel and hear.

Factors our team considered

  • Accessibility first: screen readers, keyboard, touch, and audio legends before listening.
  • Scientific honesty: calibrated values, values the visuals can't show (low CO₂, cold ocean background) left silent, dates labelled "about", and documented limitations.
  • Musicality versus accuracy: scale snapping, voice limits and the limiter.
  • Performance: lookup tables and small analysis grids for real-time speed on phones.
  • Validation: automated tests on real frames against known patterns (warmest water in the tropics, dust over the Sahara, no lightning outside the ISS orbit band).
  • Credits and transparency: NASA SVS credits, plus disclosure of AI assistance and AI-generated images.
